description: What each vitamin and mineral does, signs of low levels, food sources and NHS advice. Daily intakes and upper limits are in daily_needs.json.

vitamin_a.name: Vitamin A
what_it_does: Helps your immune system work properly
Helps you see in dim light
Keeps skin and the lining of some parts of the body, such as the nose, healthy
signs_of_low_levels: Getting infections more often, such as chest infections
food_sources: Oily fish, such as salmon, sardines, trout, herring and mackerel
Liver and liver pâté (very rich in vitamin A; avoid if pregnant)
Foods with beta-carotene, which the body turns into vitamin A: carrots, sweet potatoes, spinach, red peppers, mango, papaya and apricots
advice: Don't have more than 1,500µg (1.5mg) a day from food and supplements combined.
If you eat liver or liver pâté, have it no more than once a week, and don't take supplements containing vitamin A, including fish liver oil.
If you're pregnant, don't take cod liver oil or supplements containing vitamin A (retinol), and avoid liver, because too much vitamin A can harm a baby's development.
Women past the menopause and older men should take extra care to stay under 1,500µg a day, as too much over many years may weaken bones.
Your body stores vitamin A, so you don't need it every day.

vitamin_b1.name: Vitamin B1 (thiamin)
what_it_does: Helps your body break down and release energy from food
Keeps your nervous system healthy
signs_of_low_levels: Loss of appetite and weight loss
Tingling or numbness in the hands and feet (when levels are very low)
advice: Your body can't store thiamin, so you need some every day.

vitamin_b2.name: Vitamin B2 (riboflavin)
what_it_does: Keeps skin, eyes and the nervous system healthy
Helps your body release energy from food
signs_of_low_levels: Sores or cracks at the corners of the mouth
advice: Your body can't store riboflavin, so you need some every day.
UV light destroys riboflavin, so keep these foods out of direct sunlight.

vitamin_b3.name: Vitamin B3 (niacin)
what_it_does: Helps your body release energy from food
Keeps your nervous system and skin healthy
signs_of_low_levels: Rough skin that turns red or brown in the sun
Stomach upsets, such as sickness, constipation or diarrhoea
advice: Your body can't store niacin, so you need some every day.
Serious niacin deficiency is uncommon in countries like the UK.
Niacin comes in two forms, nicotinic acid and nicotinamide. High doses of nicotinic acid can cause skin flushing, and taking them for a long time could damage the liver.

vitamin_b6.name: Vitamin B6
what_it_does: Helps your body use and store energy from protein and carbohydrates
Helps your body make haemoglobin, which carries oxygen in red blood cells
signs_of_low_levels: Scaly skin on the lips, or cracks at the corners of the mouth
advice: Don't take more than 10mg a day in supplements unless a doctor advises it.
Taking 200mg or more a day can cause loss of feeling in the arms and legs. This usually gets better when the supplements stop, but can occasionally be permanent.

vitamin_b9.name: Vitamin B9 (folate)
what_it_does: Helps your body make healthy red blood cells
Lowers the risk of neural tube defects, such as spina bifida, in unborn babies
signs_of_low_levels: A sore or red tongue, sometimes with mouth ulcers
food_sources: Leafy greens, such as cabbage, kale, spring greens and spinach
Breakfast cereals fortified with folic acid
advice: Folic acid is the man-made form of folate, used in supplements and fortified foods.
If you're pregnant, trying for a baby or could get pregnant, take a 400µg folic acid supplement every day until you're 12 weeks pregnant.
Some women at higher risk are prescribed a 5mg dose by a GP instead.
Your body doesn't store folate for long, so eat folate-rich foods often.
Folic acid doses above 1mg a day can hide the signs of vitamin B12 deficiency. This matters more for older people.

vitamin_b12.name: Vitamin B12
what_it_does: Helps make red blood cells
Keeps your nervous system healthy
Helps your body release energy from food and use folate
advice: B12 isn't found naturally in fruit, vegetables or grains, so vegans may need a supplement.
Vegan sources include breakfast cereals and unsweetened soya drinks fortified with B12, and yeast extract (such as Marmite) or nutritional yeast flakes fortified with B12.
Absorbing B12 gets harder as you get older.

vitamin_c.name: Vitamin C
what_it_does: Helps protect cells and keep them healthy
Keeps skin, blood vessels, bones and cartilage healthy
Helps wounds heal
signs_of_low_levels: Bruising easily, or red or blue spots on the skin
advice: Your body can't store vitamin C, so you need some every day.
Eating vitamin C-rich foods at the same meal helps your body absorb iron from plant foods.
More than 1,000mg a day from supplements can cause stomach pain, diarrhoea and wind. This goes away when the supplements stop.

vitamin_d.name: Vitamin D
what_it_does: Helps control the amount of calcium and phosphate in the body
Keeps bones, teeth and muscles healthy
signs_of_low_levels: Pain in the back, ribs, pelvis or legs
Weak muscles, such as finding it hard to climb stairs or get out of a chair
food_sources: Sunlight on your skin, from late March or early April to the end of September
Oily fish, such as salmon, sardines, trout, herring and mackerel
Fortified foods, such as some fat spreads and breakfast cereals
advice: Between October and early March the UK sun isn't strong enough to make vitamin D, so everyone, including pregnant and breastfeeding women, should consider a 10µg supplement every day.
Take a 10µg supplement every day all year if you're rarely outdoors (for example housebound or living in a care home) or usually cover most of your skin when outside.
People with dark skin, such as those of African, African-Caribbean or south Asian background, may not make enough from sunlight and should consider 10µg a day all year.
Children aged 1 to 4 should have a 10µg supplement every day all year. Babies under 1 need 8.5 to 10µg a day if breastfed or having less than 500ml of formula a day.
UK cows' milk isn't a good source, because it usually isn't fortified.
Vegan sources include fortified fat spreads, breakfast cereals and unsweetened soya drinks with vitamin D added.
1µg is 40 IU, so 10µg is 400 IU.
You can't get too much vitamin D from sunlight, but taking too much in supplements over a long time can raise calcium levels and damage bones, kidneys and the heart.
Some medical conditions mean people can't safely take as much. If a doctor recommends a different amount, follow their advice.
Some people can get free vitamin supplements through Healthy Start.

vitamin_e.name: Vitamin E
what_it_does: Helps keep skin and eyes healthy
Strengthens your immune system
signs_of_low_levels: Loss of feeling in the arms and legs
Loss of control of body movements
food_sources: Plant oils, such as rapeseed (vegetable), sunflower, soya, corn and olive oil
Wheatgerm, found in cereals and cereal products
advice: Low vitamin E is very rare in healthy people. It's usually linked to conditions that affect how the body absorbs fat.
Your body stores vitamin E, so you don't need it every day.
540mg of vitamin E is 800 IU.

vitamin_k.name: Vitamin K
what_it_does: Needed for blood clotting, which helps wounds heal
There's some evidence it may help keep bones healthy
signs_of_low_levels: Bleeding that takes longer than usual to stop
food_sources: Green leafy vegetables, such as broccoli and spinach
Small amounts in meat and dairy foods
advice: Adults need about 1µg a day for each kilogram of body weight. For example, someone weighing 65kg needs about 65µg a day.
Your liver stores vitamin K, so you don't need it every day.
If you take warfarin, don't take vitamin K supplements. Foods high in vitamin K, such as green leafy vegetables, can affect how warfarin works, so ask your warfarin clinic for advice.

iron.name: Iron
what_it_does: Helps make red blood cells, which carry oxygen around the body
food_sources: Beans, such as red kidney beans, edamame beans and chickpeas
Dried fruit, such as dried apricots
advice: Women aged 19 to 49 need more iron than men. Women still having periods after 50 may need the same amount as younger women.
Iron from plant foods is absorbed less well than iron from meat. Eat vitamin C-rich foods at the same meal, and avoid tea or coffee with or straight after main meals.

Vegan sources include pulses, wholemeal bread and flour, iron-fortified cereals, dark green leafy vegetables such as watercress, broccoli and spring greens, nuts, and dried fruit such as apricots, prunes and figs.
Women with heavy periods are more likely to have low iron. A GP or dietitian can advise.
In pregnancy, iron levels are checked at the booking appointment and at around 28 weeks.
Iron supplements can be fatal to children in large amounts, so keep them out of children's reach.
The Department of Health and Social Care advises limiting red and processed meat.

calcium.name: Calcium
what_it_does: Helps build bones and keep teeth healthy
Controls muscle contractions, including your heartbeat
Helps blood clot normally
signs_of_low_levels: Over time, weak or fragile bones that break more easily
Bone pain in the back, ribs, pelvis or legs
In children, problems with bone growth (rickets)
food_sources: Milk, cheese and other dairy foods
Green leafy vegetables, such as curly kale and okra (but not spinach)
Bread and anything made with fortified flour
Fish where you eat the bones, such as sardines and pilchards
advice: Spinach contains calcium, but your body can't absorb much of it.
Vegan sources include fortified unsweetened soya, pea and oat drinks, calcium-set tofu, sesame seeds and tahini, pulses, bread, dried fruit and green leafy vegetables.
Vitamin D helps control calcium in the body, so both matter for healthy bones.

magnesium.name: Magnesium
what_it_does: Helps turn the food you eat into energy
Helps the parathyroid glands work normally. They make hormones that are important for bone health.
signs_of_low_levels: Numbness, tingling or muscle cramps (when levels are very low)
advice: A short spell of low magnesium usually causes no obvious symptoms.

zinc.name: Zinc
what_it_does: Helps make new cells and enzymes
Helps your body process carbohydrate, fat and protein in food
Helps wounds heal
advice: High doses of zinc reduce how much copper your body can absorb, which can lead to anaemia and weaker bones.

potassium.name: Potassium
what_it_does: Helps control the balance of fluids in the body
Helps your heart muscle work properly
food_sources: Vegetables, such as broccoli, parsnips and brussels sprouts
advice: Most foods contain some potassium.
Older people shouldn't take potassium supplements unless a doctor advises it, as their kidneys may not clear extra potassium well.
People with chronic kidney disease should avoid potassium supplements.
